summary: This experimental document defines how CoAP should be used in group communication. Constrained devices often work in groups, such as all lights in a room, so a single request can target many devices at once.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of telling each light to turn on, shout once and every light in the room listens. This RFC explains how small devices can be controlled as a group.

questions: control all lights at once coap
how does multicast work in coap
subtitle: Using IP multicast to control multiple constrained devices with a single message

tldr.problem: Constrained devices such as lights and sensors often work in groups, and controlling each device individually is inefficient. Group communication with a single message to many devices would save bandwidth and latency.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7390 defines how to send CoAP requests over IP multicast to reach multiple devices in a group, with each device sending back individual unicast responses. It includes mechanisms for membership management, congestion control, and rules for when devices should respond.
tldr.outcome: Constrained networks can now efficiently control large groups of devices, such as turning on all lights in a building or reading all thermostats in a wing, with a single request. This is an experimental design that sees deployment in building automation.

today: RFC 7390 is an Experimental protocol. It defines the specification for CoAP group communication using IP multicast and has been implemented in various IoT frameworks. The specification is used in real deployments such as building automation systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) is a web protocol designed for resource-limited devices running on slow, lossy networks. When many such devices work together—such as all the lights in a room or all the thermostats in a building—a CoAP client often needs to communicate with multiple devices at once.

This RFC specifies how to use CoAP with IP multicast, a network feature that lets a single message reach multiple recipients. Instead of the client sending separate unicast requests to each device ("turn on light 1, turn on light 2, turn on light 3"), it sends a single multicast request that all lights receive. Each light responds individually back to the client with a unicast message.

The approach is based on Any Source Multicast (ASM), meaning any node can send to a multicast group, not just designated sources. CoAP group communication assumes the network does not encrypt or authenticate multicast traffic, matching the security model of the base CoAP protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: CoAP is a protocol for small devices. Group communication means sending one message to control many devices at once instead of talking to each one separately. IP multicast is the technology that makes this possible.

sections.title: Group Definition and Multicast Basics
sections.content:
A CoAP group is a set of devices that share the same IP multicast address. Each device in the group is configured to listen on that address and respond to requests sent to it. A device may belong to multiple groups at once, and membership can change dynamically.

All CoAP servers should join the "All CoAP Nodes" multicast group by default. For IPv4, this is the address 224.0.1.187; for IPv6, devices join both ff02::fd (link-local) and ff05::fd (site-local).

A group URI looks like coap://224.0.1.187/lights, combining a multicast address with a resource path. The client can also use a hostname—for example, coap://all.floor1.west.bldg6.example.com/lights—which the network resolves to the multicast address. All devices in the group must use the same port (default 5683) and the same resource path; otherwise, they will not respond to the same group request.
sections.plainLanguage: A group is like a chat room: each device listens on the same multicast address, like a phone number everyone shares. When the client sends a message to that address, all listeners get it.

sections.title: Request, Response, and Congestion Control
sections.content:
All group requests must be sent as Non-confirmable messages; confirmable requests with retries would overwhelm the network. Each request carries a unique token so the client can match responses to the original request, even if multiple responses arrive.

Because the number of responses from a multicast request is not known in advance, there are strict rules about reusing token values. The client must wait longer than 500 seconds before reusing a token (the default, calculated as NON_LIFETIME + MAX_LATENCY + 250 seconds for maximum server delay). The safest approach is to generate a fresh token for every multicast request.

Individual devices can suppress responses they would normally send. For example, in a lighting control scenario, all devices might suppress success responses (leaving only errors), reducing network traffic. The RFC defines response suppression rules: servers may skip responding if there's nothing useful to report, or may implement per-resource configuration to suppress certain response types (2.xx success, 4.xx client errors, 5.xx server errors, or empty payloads).

To prevent congestion, servers should use Leisure—a random delay before responding—and limit multicast support to specific resources. Servers on low-power networks should only support group GET for small resources (payload under 5% of the network MTU).
sections.plainLanguage: When a client shouts to a group, it gets back many answers, but not in the same way as a one-to-one conversation. Servers wait a random time before responding to avoid everyone answering at once and causing a traffic jam.

sections.title: Membership Management
sections.content:
Devices can learn their group memberships in several ways: preconfigured at deployment, discovered via service discovery or the Resource Directory, or configured dynamically by a commissioning tool (such as during building installation).

For standardized management, the RFC defines a CoAP Group Configuration RESTful interface, typically at the path /coap-group. This allows authorized clients (via TLS) to manage which multicast groups a device joins. Each group membership is a JSON object with an optional name (hostname or FQDN) and an IP multicast address with optional port.

For example, a commissioning tool might POST a new membership: { "n": "lights.floor1.bldg6", "a": "[ff15::4200:f7fe:ed37:abcd]:5683" }, and the device then joins that multicast group. A client can later GET all memberships, update or delete individual ones using unicast operations before the multicast requests begin.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices need to know which groups to listen to. An authorized tool can tell each device "join this group" using secure HTTP-like commands before the group communication starts.

sections.title: Deployment and Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC covers deployment scenarios on different network types. In a 6LoWPAN (low-power wireless) network with a border router, multicast forwarding needs special handling. RPL (IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power networks) or MPL (Multicast Protocol for Low-Power networks) can route multicast within constrained networks.

A concrete example: a lighting control system in a building. A light switch acts as a client, sending a multicast PUT request to the group coap://lights.floor1/state. All lights on floor 1 receive the request, update their state, and (per configuration) may suppress success responses to avoid network congestion. If response suppression is disabled, the controller collects responses to confirm which lights executed the command.

The RFC also discusses how a Resource Directory can help applications discover which groups exist and their members, enabling service discovery at a larger scale than simple multicast within a link.
sections.plainLanguage: In a real building, a light switch sends one command to turn on all the lights in the room at once. Different types of networks (wireless, wired) need slightly different rules for the message to reach everyone.
